title: Deadlocks, without the guesswork

pages.text: A deadlock is a state in which a set of threads cannot proceed because each waits for a resource held by another in the set. Four necessary conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait. Removing any one condition prevents this kind of deadlock.

Suppose there is exactly one instance of each resource. Thread A holds lock X and requests Y. Thread B holds Y and requests X. Neither releases its held lock until it obtains the other. Both remain blocked. A cycle does not always imply deadlock when a resource has multiple instances.

Deadlock prevention disallows at least one necessary condition by design. For example, all threads acquire X before Y, preventing a circular wait between these two locks. Avoidance instead examines proposed allocations and grants only those that preserve a safe completion sequence. Prevention and avoidance are different strategies.

concepts.title: The four conditions
concepts.quote: A deadlock is a state in which a set of threads cannot proceed because each waits for a resource held by another in the set. Four necessary conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait. Removing any one condition prevents this kind of deadlock.
concepts.plain: Imagine two people each holding one key and waiting for the other key. A deadlock needs exclusive resources, holding while waiting, no forced taking-away, and a waiting loop. Remove one ingredient and this deadlock cannot form.
concepts.example: If a thread must obtain all required locks together, it cannot hold one lock while waiting for another: hold-and-wait is removed.

concepts.title: Spot the waiting loop
concepts.quote: Suppose there is exactly one instance of each resource. Thread A holds lock X and requests Y. Thread B holds Y and requests X. Neither releases its held lock until it obtains the other. Both remain blocked. A cycle does not always imply deadlock when a resource has multiple instances.
concepts.plain: Follow who is waiting for whom. A waits for B, and B waits for A. In our examples every lock has one instance and a blocked thread does not release its lock. Both wait forever unless something outside changes the state.
concepts.example: A holds X -> waits for Y held by B -> B waits for X held by A. The arrow loop is the evidence. With multiple interchangeable instances, a cycle alone is not enough.

concepts.title: Prevent or avoid?
concepts.quote: Deadlock prevention disallows at least one necessary condition by design. For example, all threads acquire X before Y, preventing a circular wait between these two locks. Avoidance instead examines proposed allocations and grants only those that preserve a safe completion sequence. Prevention and avoidance are different strategies.
concepts.plain: Prevention changes the rules so a necessary ingredient cannot happen. Avoidance checks a particular allocation before allowing it, making sure all threads could still finish in some order.
concepts.example: Always take X before Y = prevention. Simulate an allocation and check a safe finishing order = avoidance.

pre.prompt: A thread holds a printer while waiting for a scanner. Which condition is illustrated?
pre.why: It keeps one resource while waiting for another.

pre.prompt: Which change rules out one necessary deadlock condition?
options: Require all needed locks to be obtained together
Increase the waiting timeout without releasing locks
pre.why: Obtaining all locks together removes hold-and-wait.

pre.prompt: One instance each: A holds X and waits for Y; B holds Y and waits for X. Neither releases while blocked. What follows?
options: There is not enough information because the locks have names
pre.why: The two held locks and circular waiting leave neither thread able to proceed.

pre.prompt: A waiting cycle with several interchangeable instances per resource proves deadlock. Is this always true?
pre.why: With multiple instances, a cycle is not sufficient by itself.

pre.prompt: Every thread must acquire X before Y. This is:
pre.why: A fixed lock order prevents circular wait.

pre.prompt: Checking whether an allocation leaves a safe completion order is:
pre.why: Avoidance checks the safety of an allocation.

practice.prompt: A lock can be forcibly reclaimed. Which necessary condition is broken?
Single-instance locks: E owns P and wants Q; F owns Q but needs nothing else. Is deadlock established?
practice.why: F can finish and release Q, so there is no closed waiting loop.

practice.prompt: Why can a universal lock order help?
options: It prevents a circular waiting order
It removes the need for testing
practice.why: An agreed acquisition order prevents circular wait; it does not guarantee speed.

post.prompt: A task retains a database lock while requesting a file lock. Name the condition.
post.why: A retained resource plus a pending request illustrates hold-and-wait.

post.prompt: A system permits a task to request resources only when it holds none. What does this remove?
post.why: It cannot hold a resource while requesting another.

post.prompt: Single-instance locks: C holds M and waits for N; D holds N and waits for M. No forced release is possible. What is the state?
post.why: Each waits for the only instance held by the other.

post.prompt: A graph cycle involves resource types with multiple instances. What can you conclude from the cycle alone?
post.why: A cycle alone is insufficient when a resource has multiple instances.

post.prompt: All workers request lock A before lock B. Which strategy is used?
post.why: The ordering rule removes circular wait.

post.prompt: Before granting a request, simulate whether all workers can still finish in some order. This is:
post.why: Safe-state checking is avoidance, not a claim about performance.

references.title: OSTEP: Common Concurrency Problems
references.note: Reference for four necessary conditions and lock ordering. Sample prose and questions are original.

limitations: Original sample content, source-checked but not expert-reviewed.
Six items per assessment; two per concept. Forms match a blueprint but are not statistically equated.
Single-instance resource examples only. No claim of lasting mastery or causal learning benefit.

recall.prompt: A task can have its resource forcibly taken away. Which necessary condition no longer holds?
recall.why: No preemption means resources cannot be forcibly taken. This system permits that.

recall.prompt: A service can request another lock only after it releases every lock it owns. Which condition does this rule remove?
recall.why: The service cannot hold one resource while waiting for another.

recall.prompt: One copy each: T owns R, waits for S; U owns S, waits for R. Both keep their locks and requests block. What follows?
recall.why: The closed wait cycle leaves neither thread with a way to proceed.

recall.prompt: T waits for a lock owned by U. U needs no further locks and can finish. Is a closed deadlock cycle established?
recall.why: U can finish and release the lock, allowing T to continue. A wait is not by itself a cycle.

recall.prompt: Every worker must use the same increasing lock order. What does this prevent?
recall.why: A universal acquisition order prevents circular wait, not every wait or delay.

recall.prompt: A scheduler tentatively allocates resources and searches for an order in which all tasks can finish. Which strategy is this?
options: Prevention by removing all resource sharing
recall.why: Checking the safety of a proposed allocation is avoidance.

lab.intro: A wait is not always a deadlock. Build a state, predict whether a closed cycle exists, then inspect the reasoning.
lab.assumptions: One instance per lock; non-reentrant locks; blocking requests; each thread has at most one pending request. Threads keep held locks while blocked. A thread with no blocker can finish and release its locks. This is not a general Banker's-algorithm simulator.

summary: The four conditions, waiting cycles, and prevention vs avoidance. For learners who get stuck on dense concurrency notes.
